term: git status / add / commit / log / diff

def: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary, letting a function take a flexible number of inputs.
A text file (usually `README.md`) at the top of a repository that explains what the project is and how to use it.
A request on GitHub to merge one branch's commits into another, reviewed (even by yourself) before it merges.
A file named `Makefile` listing named targets and the shell commands each one runs; `make target` runs them, skipping work that is already up to date.
One numbered step of the project's own pipeline plan (stage 1, stage 2, ...); each stage corresponds to one or more of the numbered scripts.
Training a model on examples that already have the right answer attached; classification is supervised learning where the answer is one of a fixed set of categories.
A wire coil buried in the pavement that senses a vehicle passing over it by the change it causes in a magnetic field; most PeMS stations use a pair of these.
A sequence of values for the same thing, in time order, one entry per time step, like one station's speed reading every five minutes for a month.
A pattern written in a small symbolic language for matching and pulling text out of a string, like finding "I-880" inside "Collision on I-880 N".
HTTP is the request-and-response language a program uses to talk to a web server; a URL is the address of what you're asking for, like `https://511.org/traffic`.
A rectangle described by its min and max latitude and longitude, used to test whether a point (like an incident) falls inside an area (like Fremont).
A pattern like `*.csv` that the shell expands into every matching filename before running the command, so `*` stands for "anything."
`with expr as name:` runs setup before the indented block and guaranteed cleanup after it, even if the block raises an error; `with open(path) as f:` is the common example.
The power you'd raise a fixed base to, to get a number; ln is log base e, and it turns multiplying into adding.
Two unrelated uses of the same Greek letter: capital Σ means "add up a list"; lowercase σ usually means standard deviation, but inside σ(z) it means the sigmoid function instead.
∂f/∂x is the derivative of f with respect to x alone, treating every other input as if it were frozen; the gradient collects one per input.
A function shaped like a single bowl, with no separate dips; every local minimum is also the global minimum, so gradient descent can't get stuck.
numpy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by automatically stretching the smaller one, so `X @ w + b` can add one bias number to every row of X without a loop.
`1e-6` means 1 × 10⁻⁶, or 0.000001; the `e` here means "times ten to the power of," not Euler's number.
The long-run average outcome of a random quantity, weighting each possible value by how likely it is; written E[X].
A number from −1 to 1 measuring how closely two quantities move together in a straight-line way; it does not mean one causes the other.
The probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if nothing real were going on; small does not mean "true," and large does not mean "false."
A small number or letter written after a variable, like x₁ or wᵢ, that says which item in a list you mean; x₁ is the first item, x₂ the second, xᵢ a generic, unspecified one.

term: Law of large numbers / Central limit theorem
def: The law of large numbers says an average settles down toward the true value as you collect more data; the central limit theorem says that average's own error shrinks and starts looking normally distributed as it does.
The units a file or a computer's memory is measured in. A byte is about one letter of storage; kilo-, mega- and giga- each multiply it by roughly a thousand.

term: Primary key / foreign key / database index
def: A primary key is a column that uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key is a column that points to another table's primary key; an index is a lookup structure built on a column so a database can find matching rows fast.
Change a pandas time series to a coarser or finer regular interval: `resample('1h').mean()` groups five-minute rows into hourly ones.
The step-by-step plan a database will actually use to run a query. `EXPLAIN` prints it before running, so you can see whether it will scan everything or use a shortcut.
A transaction is a group of database reads and writes treated as one all-or-nothing unit. ACID names the guarantees it gets: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.
The fraction of a dataset that can be replaced with extreme values before a statistic gets dragged arbitrarily far from the truth; higher means harder to fool.
How much a number computed from a sample, like a median or mean, would wobble if recomputed from a different sample of the same size; smaller means more trustworthy.
Σ means 'add up whatever follows, once for each value of the index shown below and above it'; Π does the same but multiplies. Both are compact ways to write a loop.
Heteroscedastic means how noisy or spread-out the data is changes depending on where you look; homoscedastic means the spread stays about the same everywhere.
A score reporting how much better a forecast is than a simple reference forecast, scaled so 0 means 'no better than the reference' and 1 means 'perfect.'
A way to approximate a curvy function near one point using a straight line, or a slightly bent curve, built from the function's value and its derivatives there.
A compact if/else that produces a value: `a if condition else b` evaluates to `a` when the condition is true and `b` otherwise, all on one line.
Lets you put two complete statements on one physical line, `x = 1; y = 2`, exactly as if they had been written on two separate lines.
A loss function that automatically down-weights examples the model already gets right and confident, so training spends its effort on the hard, still-wrong ones; used to fight severe class imbalance.
The fraction of the target's variance a regression model explains; 1 is a perfect fit, 0 is no better than guessing the mean, and it can go negative.
A regularized linear model that mixes ridge's L2 penalty and lasso's L1 penalty, controlled by a knob that slides between them.
Two ways to combine a per-class metric like precision or recall into one number: macro treats every class equally, micro treats every row equally.
As the number of features grows, points spread out and distances between them stop being meaningful, which breaks any method that relies on 'nearby' points being similar.
Two ways to pick k, the number of clusters: the elbow method looks for diminishing returns; the silhouette score measures how well-separated the clusters actually are.
Two clustering methods needing no k ahead of time: DBSCAN groups by density, marking sparse points noise; hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges, cuttable anywhere.
An anomaly detector that builds random decision trees and flags a point as unusual if it takes very few splits to isolate it from everything else.

A direction that a matrix only stretches, never rotates (the eigenvector), and the amount it stretches by (the eigenvalue); PCA's principal components are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix.
Two techniques that squeeze high-dimensional data down to two or three dimensions for a plot, preserving which points were close neighbors rather than the overall geometry PCA preserves.
An algorithm for fitting a model with hidden, unobserved structure by alternating between guessing the hidden values and refitting the model, until it stops improving.
ARIMA extended to several time series at once, where each series is predicted from its own recent past and every other series' recent past together.
A way to split a time series into trend, seasonal and leftover pieces, robust to outliers and able to handle more than one seasonal cycle at once.
Two ways to predict several steps ahead: direct trains a separate model per horizon; recursive trains one model and feeds its own prediction back in for the next step.
Hyperparameter-search methods that run many trials with a small budget each, then keep only the best-performing ones and give them a bigger budget, repeating until one trial wins.
A method for tracking a hidden, changing quantity over time from noisy measurements, blending a prediction of where it should be with each new noisy reading.
Classifying into categories that have a real order (light < moderate < heavy), penalizing being off by one category less than being off by two, unlike ordinary multiclass loss.
Testing a forecasting model by repeatedly moving the train/test split forward in time, so every fold trains only on the past and tests only on what comes after it.
Forecast-error metrics divided by a naive baseline's error, so a score below 1 means the model beats naive guessing and scores are comparable across very different series.
The rule for picking a network's very first, random weights, scaled so early activations and gradients stay neither tiny nor huge.
A way to fine-tune a huge pretrained model cheaply by training only a small pair of add-on matrices instead of all its weights.
A generative model built from a chain of invertible transformations, turning noise into data (and back) while computing an exact likelihood.
A language model's evaluation score: roughly, how surprised the model is by held-out text, on average, per token. Lower is better.
A further training step that adjusts a language model using people's judgments of which of two answers is better, rather than one correct answer.
When fine-tuning a model on a new task overwrites what it previously learned, so its performance on the old task collapses.
A data structure built over embedding vectors that quickly finds the ones most similar to a query, used to fetch relevant documents for retrieval-augmented generation.
Splitting a long document into smaller pieces before turning each into an embedding, so retrieval can find and return just the relevant part.
The power you would raise a fixed base to in order to get a number; ln uses base e (about 2.718), and log(...) in this course's formulas usually means ln too.
Σ means 'add up everything that follows, once for each value of an index'; a subscript like xᵢ or pᵢ just numbers which item in a list is meant.
A server is a program that stays running and waits for requests instead of exiting after one command; an endpoint is one specific URL on that server that answers a specific kind of request.
A number, 0 to 65535, that identifies which program on a machine a network connection is for, the way an apartment number identifies which door at one street address.
One running instance of a program, with its own memory and its own place in line for the computer's attention; the operating system can run many processes at once.
A whole simulated computer, with its own operating system, running inside a real one; renting one by the hour is the basic building block of 'the cloud.'
A cloud service that stores files, called objects, under simple names, reachable by any number of machines over the network, instead of living on one machine's disk.

A tracked, versioned store of trained models, the files plus metadata about how each was made and how it scored, so a service can point at 'the current one' and roll back to an older one on demand; not the same as this course's own PeMS station Registry.

Two short standard documents: a model card describes what a model is for, how it was evaluated and where it fails; a datasheet describes how a dataset was collected, what it contains, and how it should and should not be used.
A command-line tool that sends a request to a URL and prints back what the server answers, the terminal equivalent of typing an address into a browser.
Disk space the operating system uses as overflow memory when RAM fills up; using it makes a program dramatically slower because disk is much slower than RAM.
A hidden variable that causes both the thing you're calling the treatment and the thing you're calling the outcome, making them look related even if one doesn't actually cause the other.

A causal diagram, or DAG, draws an arrow from every cause to its direct effects; a collider is a variable that two arrows point into, and conditioning on one creates a fake association between its causes.

A multi-armed bandit is the simplest reinforcement-learning setup, repeatedly choosing among a fixed set of options with unknown payoffs; UCB and Thompson sampling are two strategies for deciding when to keep trying an option versus switch to a better-looking one.

A mathematical guarantee that a released statistic would look almost the same whether or not any one specific person's data was included, controlled by a number epsilon: smaller epsilon means stronger privacy and more noise.
A ranking metric that rewards putting the most relevant items near the top of a list, discounting items further down, and normalizing so a perfect ranking always scores 1.

Different mathematical definitions of a 'fair' model that generally cannot all hold at once: demographic parity means every group gets flagged at the same rate; equalized odds, or equal error rates, means every group has the same true- and false-positive rate; calibration means a score means the same real chance of the outcome in every group.
A fixed set of requests one program is allowed to send another and the answers it will get back, so two programs can talk without either seeing the other's code.
Two functions that read off the horizontal and vertical position of a point walking around a circle, used whenever something repeats in a cycle, like the hours in a day.
